entries.title: Schumer Super PAC Drops $2 Million in Senate Democrats’ First Texas Spend
entries.summary: The amount pales compared to the $130 million Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s super PAC has spent so far in the state.
entries.content:
A new arm of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s political committee on Thursday disclosed $2.1 million in spending on an ad against Texas Republican Ken Paxton. It’s the first major spending by Democratic leadership in the state’s Senate race — but a drop in the bucket compared to Republicans’ investments over the past month.

The Senate Majority PAC’s affiliate committee, Texas Forever, spent the money on a digital ad that dropped Tuesday. The spot addresses Paxton’s handling of a controversial plea deal in a high-profile child sex abuse case, in which the state attorney general reduced former Waco defense attorney Adam Hoffman’s charges in exchange for his guilty pleas of sexually abusing his son’s friend.

“Ken Paxton is dangerously corrupt for Texas,” the ad says, saying Paxton awarded Hoffman an “Epstein-style deal to let a pedophile walk free.”

The new ad buy pales in comparison to Republicans’ spending in the state — particularly by Senate Majority Leader John Thune, whose Senate Leadership Fund super PAC has disclosed $130 million in Texas spending since September, a number that will likely balloon as Nov. 3 draws closer.

Spending habits in the state reflect intertwining anxieties within both parties about Democrats’ chances of winning a Senate seat for the first time since 1988.

Democrats historically haven’t spent significant amounts of money in Texas’ expensive media market, and the party is currently facing a major cash crunch. But the National Republican Senatorial Committee and Thune’s super PAC have also had to increasingly direct more resources to what should be a reliably red seat, especially as state Rep. James Talarico maintains a tight polling lead.

President Donald Trump kicked off his ambitious midterm campaign blitz in Durant, Oklahoma, and Denton, Texas, on Thursday in hopes of amplifying Republicans’ accomplishments in already red states.

But even the president’s preferred candidate hasn’t garnered much enthusiasm: Despite party leaders’ pleas for him to get more financially involved in the tight race, Trump has only disclosed spending about $20 million for Paxton, whom he endorsed over Sen. John Cornyn this spring.

“He can be a pain in the ass sometimes, I’ll be honest,” Trump said while praising Paxton during his Texas speech Thursday, asking if the state attorney general was even in the room. “Oh, there he is. I didn’t even know if he’s here — I don’t care.”

entries.title: MLB Drops the Idea for a Game at Grand Teton National Park
entries.summary: Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred said local opposition prompted the decision.
entries.content:
MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred on Thursday scrapped an idea to field a baseball game in Grand Teton National Park after locals rejected the league’s interest as “hostile” to public lands.

In a letter to Wyoming officials Thursday, Manfred minimized the plan as one option among “literally scores” of venues considered by the league. MLB officials had contacted the Trump administration about staging a game at a national park “similar to the Field of Dreams game,” according to the White House. An official from the National Park Service had already made a trip to Grand Teton to scout potential sites before pressure from local officials forced Manfred to abandon the idea.

“We obviously would not bring a game to a community that has concerns about the venue, and we will not continue to evaluate Grand Teton National Park as a potential site,” he wrote in the Thursday letter, first reported by The Washington Post.

An MLB official declined to comment Thursday night.

“This is not a Presidential directive, nor is it being directed by the White House,” a White House spokesperson told The Washington Sun on Sunday. “It’s also not being driven by the Department of Interior.”

The league has hosted several games at nontraditional venues — including one at the historic Negro League ballpark in Birmingham, Alabama, and another at Fort Bragg in North Carolina — Manfred wrote, adding, “We have been careful to leave the selected sites better than when we arrived.”

He characterized the inquiry into Grand Teton as “initial due diligence.”

Teton County Commissioner Luther Propst said that he first spotted Frank Lands, a deputy director for the National Park Service, at Grand Teton last week.

The Teton County Commission and the Jackson Town Council unanimously approved draft letters on Monday objecting to the baseball game idea, Propst said.

“It crystallizes these issues in a way that everybody can understand — that the Trump administration is undertaking a very hostile approach to managing public lands,” Propst said Thursday night.

“It’s a war on our public lands,” he added. “This one we won, but every month there are another dozen assaults.”

In August, The Sun reported that officials within the Trump administration had lobbied the National Park Service regarding a potential land exchange benefitting a private developer who sought to construct an access road between an external property and Yosemite National Park.

entries.title: What Happened to $300 Million in Taiwan Aid? It’s Classified.
entries.summary: The Trump administration’s secrecy over the funding comes days after the president’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
entries.content:
The Trump administration has classified its accounting of what happened to $300 million in military aid Congress provided for Taiwan, leaving lawmakers without a public answer about whether the money was ultimately committed after a Sept. 30 deadline, according to four people familiar with the matter.

The classification obscures the administration’s handling of the Taiwan aid money just days after President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. Lawmakers in both parties have previously voiced concerns that Trump could use U.S. security assistance for Taiwan — something the president has called “a very good negotiating chip” — as leverage in talks with Beijing.

The Trump administration undertook a broad, monthslong freeze on security aid to Taiwan after Trump’s summit with Xi in May. The frozen funds included the $300 million in foreign military financing, another $1 billion provided through the Pentagon’s Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative and a $14 billion weapons package.

Now the classification is constraining lawmakers and aides from speaking publicly about what happened to at least one part of that assistance.

“I don’t know how to answer it without breaking the law,” Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee responsible for the State Department budget, said when asked about the money.

The State Department submitted a required justification to Congress for its handling of the $300 million in foreign military financing, according to the four people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations. The program allows partners to purchase U.S. defense equipment.

Because the administration classified the status of the funding, it remains unclear whether officials preserved it through another mechanism or allowed it to expire on Wednesday.

The lack of transparency is colliding with a bipartisan push on Capitol Hill to keep military support flowing to Taipei, with lawmakers pressing the administration before and after Xi’s visit last week to release congressionally approved aid and move the stalled arms sales.

“I've been instrumental in trying to get it released,” Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) told The Washington Sun, adding that she would be “appalled” if security aid to Taiwan became a bargaining chip between Trump and Xi.

An Office of Management and Budget database showed Thursday that $2.2 billion in 2026 fiscal year foreign military financing, including the $300 million intended for Taiwan, had not been committed. The account also lacked the notation OMB typically uses to indicate that an apportionment includes a classified attachment.

A senior administration official said Trump has said he will make a determination on a new Taiwan arms sale package in a short time. Trump, the official said, has approved more arms sales to Taiwan than any other president in history.

A State Department spokesperson did not comment on the aid directly but noted that Trump and Secretary Marco Rubio have said U.S. policy on Taiwan “has not changed.”

“We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan,” the statement said.

Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, criticized the broader freeze on Taiwan security aid.

“Our security commitments to Taiwan are law, not optional,” Coons said in a statement to The Washington Sun. “In the face of Chinese aggression in the region, Congress has approved billions for Taiwan’s defense that the Trump White House blocked to appease the Chinese government. That’s not how our national security should work.”

The lack of a public accounting stands in contrast with another pot of security assistance that faced the same end-of-year fiscal deadline and bipartisan pressure on the administration.

Pentagon officials told Coons on Tuesday they had obligated nearly all of the $400 million in Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative funding, just one day before that money was set to expire.

The Taiwan funding was a flashpoint before Trump met with Xi last week. Senate Republicans led by Kentucky Sen. Mitch McConnell, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, pressed the administration to move forward with all of the stalled security assistance.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) also sharpened his public pressure on the administration this week after meeting with Alexander Yui Tah-ray, Taiwan’s diplomatic representative to the United States.

“Congress has authorized and appropriated a surge in resources to provide Taiwan with enhanced training, security assistance, and arms sales,” Wicker said in a statement. “These authorities must be used for the purposes that Congress intended.”

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) — who ahead of an earlier Trump-Xi summit led a bipartisan letter reaffirming congressional support for the Taiwan Relations Act and warning against unilateral changes in U.S. policy toward Taiwan — told The Sun he was unaware the administration was not publicly explaining the disposition of the funding and didn’t see any reason for it to be kept secret.

“I feel like we need to be very clear that this is a U.S. decision,” he said. “It's not a China decision, and just as they don't want us to meddle in their internal affairs, I don't want them to meddle in ours.”

Beijing claims Taiwan as part of China and has long opposed U.S. arms sales to the self-governed island, which it says violate Chinese sovereignty and interfere with what it considers to be an internal matter. For decades, U.S. policy has balanced helping Taiwan maintain its self-defense while not explicitly supporting its independence.

Rupert Hammond-Chambers, president of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council, said several proposed arms sales to Taiwan that needed to be formally notified to Congress by Oct. 1 had not been. He declined to identify the programs, but said missing the deadline would force them back into negotiations, creating added delays and, potentially, costs.

Hammond-Chambers said the summit reinforced his view that the slowdown in U.S. weapons sales to Taiwan is connected to Trump’s negotiations with Beijing. He pointed to U.S. dependence on Chinese supplies of rare earths and other critical minerals, which has given Beijing leverage as Trump has sought to maintain a “trade truce” with Xi.

The arms sales and trade talks, Hammond-Chambers said, “are inexorably intertwined.”
entries.author: Joe Gould

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Your Dasher Is Sorry
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: DoorDash’s about-face, the Caps’ emergency goalie and the cost of cleaning up America’s birthday party.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10: Hot and humid, with increasing clouds and a late-day storm risk knocking the rating back from Thursday levels.





THE LATEST

DoorDash is delivering … an apology to D.C.

The delivery company now says it was wrong to come out in support of a Republican bill in Congress that would have restricted the city’s ability to increase taxes and fees, reports The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle.

The political dustup started over the summer, when the D.C. Council voted to impose a new 20-cent fee on all third-party deliveries. DoorDash unsuccessfully fought the fee in the Wilson Building, then sided with Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky) and his bill to rein in local lawmakers’ power to set their own tax policy.

Comer’s bill drew furious condemnation from D.C.’s elected officials, who said it would “straightjacket” the city’s governance. Advocacy group Free D.C. took aim at DoorDash, spearheading a boycott of the delivery company.

The boycott may have done the trick. On Thursday, Max Rettig, DoorDash’s head of global public policy, withdrew the company’s support for Comer’s bill. “We recognize that working directly with District leaders is the right way to fight for District residents, and that doing otherwise calls into question our commitment to D.C.,” he said.

DoorDash also said it would invest more than $1 million in helping D.C. restaurants, while at the same time calling on lawmakers to exempt SNAP food benefits recipients from the new fee, which took effect Thursday.

City officials took a bit of a victory lap in the wake of DoorDash’s announcement. “DC residents are powerful when we fight together! Our right to govern ourselves is not up for negotiation,” Democratic nominee for mayor Janeese Lewis George wrote on X. At-Large council member Robert White, who is also the Democratic nominee for D.C. delegate to Congress, used the moment to send a message: “Let this be a warning to any company considering the same playbook.”





DEEP DIVE

The Capitals’ season opens Friday night, and one of their new additions has perhaps the most fascinating job in the NHL: Connor Leslie is Washington’s first-ever full-time traveling emergency backup goalie.

Connor_Leslie_093026_0710 copy.jpg (7773x5182, AR: 1.50)The 24-year-old got the gig after fitting the extremely narrow criteria for the role (also known as an EBUG), which was established as part of the NHL’s latest collective bargaining agreement. He had to be inexperienced enough so as not to be overqualified for the role — the league didn’t want teams using the new position to sneak another professional goalie onto the roster — but good enough to be able to hold up, well, in case of emergency.

Leslie, a native of Leesburg, spent eight years training with the Washington Little Capitals before playing Division III hockey at Amherst College. He was looking for a job in federal law enforcement when he got the call asking him to take on the EBUG role, which also involves taking shots from Alex Ovechkin and Co. as a practice goalie.

“It’s pretty surreal,” Leslie told The Washington Sun’s Emma Baccellieri. “I’m over the moon about it.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

The Interior Department is paying a Maryland landscaping company almost $3.4 million to repair turf damaged during the celebrations on the National Mall for America’s 250th birthday, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. Interior also paid the company nearly $1.8 million in late June in a contract for work described as “mall fuel spill urgent cleanup.”

Amazon agreed to pay $8.25 million to settle a lawsuit with D.C. over claims the company used third-party delivery charters that resulted in slower service to predominantly Black neighborhoods. Amazon denied any wrongdoing or deception, but settled to avoid prolonged litigation, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

Advocates urged D.C.’s housing committee to strengthen landlord accountability during a five-hour hearing yesterday. Specifically, they’re seeking more transparency around who’s behind the shadowy LLCs that own and operate D.C. properties, and a fairer, faster process for abating the District’s nearly 89,000 outstanding code violations.

Perhaps it’s obvious to any D.C. resident, but Mother Jones has the data to confirm: Military flyovers above the District have surged under Donald Trump, compared to Joe Biden. There were 33 on the Fourth of July alone. It’s come at a cost: Flying just one F-35 jet for an hour can cost $40,000. Flying a B-52 for the same time can cost as much as $150,000.

Don’t let the near-90-degree weather fool you — it’s October. That means yesterday, a host of new laws took effect around the DMV. The Washington Post rounded up some, including a ban on face coverings for law enforcement officers in Maryland, more criminal records sealed in Virginia and no more pet breed restrictions for D.C. tenants.

The director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History, Kirk Johnson, is stepping down after 14 years in the role. He’ll now head up the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.





FROM MARYLAND

Montgomery County high schools are navigating “inconsistencies” in the rollout of a new policy banning students’ cellphone use not only during class, but also in hallways and at lunch, Jeff Barker writes for The Sun. Some students are complaining that the restrictions go too far, while school officials seek a uniform answer to a basic question: Where do you store all the phones?





METRO MOMENT


It’s a common scene in CVS stores across D.C.: Everyday items like toothpaste and toilet paper behind locked cabinet doors.

Retailers say they’ve had to lock away products to prevent shoplifting, but the result has often been annoyed consumers — including U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro. But she says that may now be changing in D.C.

“There is just one thing that signals a real quality-of-life improvement,” she said in a video posted to social media this week. “They are unlocking those locked cases in CVS, and that tells me that serious crime is down.”

Is CVS freeing its products? Sun reporters fanned out to find out, and came across little evidence that the retailer is moving beyond its lock-and-key approach. A CVS spokesperson was vague as to whether an edict had been handed down from corporate, saying only that “we are actively taking action to improve the experience across our national retail footprint.”

Pirro’s office didn’t respond to our inquiries about where she’d seen CVS unlocking its goods, but in the video she said she was excited with the newfound consumer freedom. “You know what I’m going to buy at CVS that’s not locked up anymore?” she asked. “Candy.”

Even that was a mixed bag, though. Some CVS stores keep their candy out in the open, even the luxe brands like Lindt chocolate. Others still don’t.

CVS Logan Circle (3878x2908, AR: 1.33)
We want to hear from you: Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it.





SPORTS

The Mystics were understandably disappointed after being eliminated from the playoffs Wednesday night, but they appear to also understand that better days lie ahead. The youngest team in the league is officially a championship contender starting next year, The Sun’s Dave Sheinin writes, with the chance to further upgrade the roster this offseason in both free agency and the draft.

“We have something special here,” says star guard Sonia Citron. “We love each other. We have fun. We never lose our joy. That’s super special. I don’t think that’s everywhere. And I’m just grateful.”

How does a plane full of pro football players handle a transatlantic flight to London? Not that much better than the rest of us, The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson writes. “I’m tired,” says edge rusher Odafe Oweh. Not even the most luxurious and spacious lie-flat seats can accommodate defensive tackle Daron Payne, who measures 6-foot-3 and 320 points.

“I’m a big guy,” Payne says. “It wasn’t really too comfortable. I might have gotten a couple hours of sleep.”

Still, Martenzie writes, the Commanders feel good about their ability to acclimate to their new surroundings and time zone ahead of Sunday’s game against the Colts. Be sure to follow Martenzie all week in London on our newly launched @washsunsports Instagram account.

What to Watch Today:

NHL: Capitals at Carolina, 7 p.m.

entries.title: Morning Sun: How to Keep Abortion Out of the Midterms
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The White House wants abortion politics to wait. The colorful description of the electoral choices in Pennsylvania. New poll finds voters want the feds’ hands off elections. Where’s Taiwan’s $300 million in aid? And: Democrats are excited about … Mississippi?





THE LATEST

Scoop: Top White House officials, led by Susie Wiles, told Todd Blanche to keep abortion off the electoral radar, The Washington Sun’s Eric Katz and Oriana González report today. The White House chief of staff indicated to the attorney general that an aggressive approach on abortion would generate unwanted attention at the moment, according to a senior administration official who was not authorized to discuss the matter publicly

“No one wants us taking any real action before the midterms,” said the official.

What our reporting shows: Cases challenging abortion pill access are making their way through the federal courts. The Trump administration is currently defending Food and Drug Administration rules that allow these drugs to be available via mail. Anti-abortion groups and allies of the movement have urged the Department of Justice to drop its procedural defense of the FDA and, instead, allow courts to rule more quickly on the merits of the cases.

The White House has made clear to Blanche that it would not support such a strategy before the election.

“This is completely false,” a White House spokesperson responded to our reporting. “These conversations never occurred between White House officials and DOJ officials.”

Multiple anti-abortion groups tell us they’ve been instructed by their Trump administration allies not to expect any aggressive action on abortion pill access until November — but to very much expect it after that. “Everything but the election is pushed until after the elections,” Kristi Hamrick of Students for Life told The Sun.

The electoral context: The end of Roe v. Wade, despite being one of Donald Trump’s most significant accomplishments, remains a dangerous political issue. Polling we revealed this week showed a majority of voters favor legal abortion access, and state-level ballot question wins by abortion rights supporters across the country in recent years bear that out.

More: MLB Drops the Idea for a Game at Grand Teton National Park • Schumer Super PAC Drops $2M in Senate Democrats’ First Texas Spend • Van Orden Hit With Cease-and-Desist Letter Over AI Deepfake Videos • Democrats Propose Bill to Cut OMB Funding if Trump Violates Anti-Propaganda Laws

Open tabs:

  • Pentagon prepares for potential surge of naval forces in Middle East (WaPo)
  • OpenAI Fires Researchers for Allegedly Sharing Information with AI Safety Group (WSJ)
  • The Fed's long-term interest rate problem (Axios)
  • Renee Good’s family sues government, top Trump officials and ICE officer who shot her (NBC)




FROM PENNSYLVANIA


Quote of the cycle? “I’m tired of the choices being between shit and diarrhea,” Keith Swiatkowski, a 48-year-old political independent who works as a butcher in the Scranton area, told The Sun’s Alex Roarty on a recent reporting trip to the district. Swiatkowski calls Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti, the Democratic nominee in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District, “a breath of fresh air.”

Alex spent time in the district to pen a story of a Democrat trying to avoid that party label at all costs. “Paige Against the Machine” is how Cognetti describes her candidacy — as in: not like other Democrats, not beholden to them. It is a story playing out in battleground districts across the country.

As is the response to it. The Republican incumbent is trying to tie Cognetti back to her party’s toxic brand. “She is certainly trying to separate herself from being the liberal progressive Democrat that she truly is,” Rep. Rob Bresnahan told Alex. “But the reality is, she is very, very far from being a moderate, middle-of-the-road person.”

On the other side of the state, it’s the Republican brand that’s the real problem. The Sun’s Paul Kane reports from Fairless Hills, where Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick or his brother Mike have not lost an election as the Republican candidate in the area of the 1st District since 2006. Brian says his name is more powerful than his party label. “I am an independent who is registered Republican,” he told Paul. He also said, “The two parties have become cults.”

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


First on The Sun: Polling shows public opposition to federal involvement in elections. A new survey out this morning from voting-access advocacy group iVote finds 74% of likely voters oppose the federal government taking over the administration of state elections, and 69% oppose the feds creating a national voter-information database from state data. The Trump administration has tried to put a tight federal leash around voting this cycle, an effort that has been partly curtailed by the courts.

Trump told Time magazine that he hadn’t ruled anything out when asked about declaring an emergency near Election Day, and demurred when asked specifically if he would send ICE agents to polling places: “Haven’t thought of it.” iVote’s polling finds 64% of likely voters oppose having ICE agents stationed at their polling location.

FROM THE PENTAGONScoop: What happened to the $300 million Congress earmarked for Taiwan? That’s classified. The Sun’s Joe Gould digs into the funding question as lawmakers press the Trump administration on why it’s obscuring where the aid money went just days after Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. Trump has previously said the security assistance is “a very good negotiating chip” to leverage in talks with Beijing.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Department of LOL, OK then: Democrats get excited in Mississippi. “I think he’s got a real shot,” Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) told The Sun of his party’s Senate nominee in Mississippi, Scott Colom. Warnock backed Colom early and now finds other top Democrats hitting the state to stump.

Our Igor Bobic reports on this fever dream longest of longshots: Some see Mississippi as the next Georgia, a sleeper purple state with a large African American population that, if engaged and motivated, can help make Democratic candidates competitive there.



More: Massachusetts Man Is Charged With Cyberstalking Former Trump Official Katie Miller • Trump Administration Sues Maryland to Stop Law Enforcement Mask Ban • Judge Rules Trump Cannot Fire Court-Appointed U.S. Attorneys





NOT US

  • What Trump Misunderstands About Modern Media, by Jake Lundberg for The Atlantic
  • Inside Larry Ellison’s Wide Web of Power, Money and Politics, by Tom Dotan for Vanity Fair

entries.title: The Democratic Brand Is a Mess. Some Democrats Are Taking Advantage.
entries.summary: Paige Cognetti, running in Pennsylvania, is one of the Democrats making the case, as one voter put it, that elections don’t need to be “between shit and diarrhea.”
entries.content:
EAST STROUDSBURG, Pa. — Paige Cognetti is trying to be the kind of Democratic candidate Republicans want to have a beer with.

It’s why her congressional campaign held a meet and greet at a local brewery here Sunday (her fourth such event) during which the candidate — dressed casually in jeans and a red-and-black flannel shirt — talked about her husband’s local sandwich shop and her “deep love of craft beer.” Or why, politically speaking, she’s perfectly happy to pick a fight with fellow Democrats if they stand in her way.

“We have to make real reforms,” she said, addressing about two-dozen potential voters before grabbing a beer herself and mingling with the crowd. “And that’s going to mean taking on both parties.”

As if to underscore her point, the 46-year-old was speaking next to a campaign sign adorned with the band-inspired slogan “Paige Against the Machine.” Cognetti coined the phrase during her 2019 independent bid for mayor of Scranton, Pennsylvania, when she defeated local Democratic candidates she viewed as part of a corrupt system.

This year, she’s attempting to take the same independent ethos and infuse it into her campaign for Pennsylvania's 8th Congressional District, running in a battleground race against Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan. Her message: She’s not like other Democrats, not beholden to them and not interested in protecting the political status quo they helped create.

The message moved at least one brewery patron: 48-year-old Keith Swiatkowski, a political independent who works as a butcher. He said he was first impressed by Cognetti when he saw a campaign ad that emphasized her differences with her party. After the two spoke, each with a beer in hand, he was sold.

“I’m tired of the choices being between shit and diarrhea,” Swiatkowski said. Gesturing toward Cognetti, he said, “This is a breath of fresh air.”

Cognetti is emblematic of a larger strategic choice from Democrats this year ahead of November’s election. Across the country, Democratic candidates are aggressively distancing themselves from a Democratic Party whose image sunk to record lows after the 2024 election, intent on portraying themselves as something different than the same old Democrat.

These candidates are playing local quinceañeras, bragging about prosecuting Democratic politicians, rejecting help from national party leaders, explicitly disowning liberal doctrine or even ditching the party label altogether. All of it’s necessary, they say, to win an election fought mostly on Republican-leaning turf, where success depends on winning over some independent and Republican-leaning voters.

“There's no question that the Democratic Party's brand is in the toilet,” said Lis Smith, a Democratic strategist, “and that running on a platform copied and pasted from national Democrats is not going to win you a seat in a tough district. But you can't manufacture independence, and voters can smell bullshit.”

Smith advises Majority Democrats, which was formed to help identify and promote Democratic candidates its leaders believe can transcend the party’s image and outperform the average candidate. Cognetti is a member of the group — and she’ll likely need to meet its aims to win her race.

Both parties view the 8th District race as part of the core House battlefield, as Democrats try to win a majority of seats in an election for the first time since 2020. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a “toss-up.”

The district, which sprawls over Pennsylvania’s northeast corner, was once a bedrock of union-supported Democrats but has turned sharply right in recent elections, with Trump winning it by over 8 percentage points in 2024. Boosted by the president, Bresnahan defeated six-term incumbent Matt Cartwright in the same election, albeit by a narrower 1.5-point margin.

It’s why, as much as Cognetti tries to portray herself as different, Republicans spend just as much time telling voters she’s simply hiding her true beliefs and is the same kind of national liberal politician they detest.

“She is certainly trying to separate herself from being the liberal progressive Democrat that she truly is,” Bresnahan told The Washington Sun in an interview. “But the reality is, she is very, very far from being a moderate, middle-of-the-road person.”

Bresnahan and his allies have attacked Cognetti over campaign donations (she received money from the Soros family), taxes (she raised property taxes as mayor of Scranton) and her career as a Democratic political operative (she worked for Hillary Clinton’s and Barack Obama’s campaigns in 2008 and served in Obama’s Treasury Department).

Lately, they’ve focused extensively on Cognetti’s birthplace, in Portland, Oregon, arguing that she’s not a local do-gooder but a West Coast liberal using northeast Pennsylvania (known in the state as NEPA) as a political stepping stone. One ad from the Congressional Leadership Fund, a GOP super PAC, literally starts calling her an “Oregon native” and “New York City transplant.”

Bresnahan has been happy to draw the contrast.

“I was born here. I went to school here. I started my career here. I got married here, and God willing, I'll die and get buried here,” he said. “I used to be on a board for a cemetery, so I know ultimately where I'm going to end up, and it's northeastern Pennsylvania.”

Republican strategists frame the race as a referendum on whether voters in the district view Cognetti as a Democrat distinct from the national party.

“If she’s Kamala Harris by Election Day, she loses this election,” said one Bresnahan adviser, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Even if she’s close to Kamala Harris, she loses this election.”

In an interview, Cognetti dismissed the Republican attacks against her, saying her record has proved her independence.

“I have a record of standing up to corruption, no matter who it is,” she said. “That's exactly what we need to do in D.C. We need to fix the system, and that's gonna take standing up to a bunch of bad practices and systemic issues that we have that benefit folks in D.C., be they Republicans or Democrats.”

Cognetti ran as an independent candidate for mayor of Scranton in 2019, running against a Democratic nominee she said had been selected through a corrupt process. The previous mayor had resigned suddenly that year and pleaded guilty to federal bribery charges, according to The Scranton Times-Tribune.

Her campaign ads have played up that history, portraying her as an independent corruption-fighter aligned with Democrats of yesteryear.

“She's different, a Democrat with a backbone like they used to make them,” says one person featured in an early ad. Another ad features a man who says he voted for Trump three times, who calls Cognetti an “old school tough gal.”

Cognetti’s policy agenda has a similar theme. She wants to ban corporate PAC money, wants 18-year term limits for members of Congress and Supreme Court justices and thinks independent voters should have a right to participate in partisan primaries. Her ads also tout how as mayor, she increased funding for police.

She said she’s not focused on potentially impeaching Donald Trump if she wins, and blamed Joe Biden’s border policy for creating a migrant crisis in Scranton and other cities across the country.

“The border was a huge problem that should have been addressed far sooner than it was,” she said.

Democrats familiar with the region say Congetti’s approach is a political no-brainer.

“If she doesn’t, she’s committing political malpractice,” said former Rep. Chris Carney, a Democrat who represented parts of the current 8th District from 2007 to 2011.

“She needs to run the way I ran in that area,” he said. “Take note that she has not campaigned with AOC, for example. She is staying as a moderate Democrat.”

Cognetti told patrons at the brewery that she had originally come to NEPA to work for Carney’s campaign in 2006, at which time she met her future husband, who was from the area.

Cognetti does tout her liberal values, too. In the same speech at the brewery, she praised Carney for supporting the Affordable Care Act in 2010, saying it cost him his career but was the right thing to do to deliver health care for the district’s citizens. She said her first priority in Congress would be restoring cuts to Medicaid enacted by the GOP congress in 2025.

Cognetti and her allies have run much of their campaign criticizing Bresnahan over a series of personal stock trades they say are interlinked with his votes on health care and the Iran war. And, as is the case across the electoral map this year, Trump’s sinking approval ratings amid the war and rising gas prices have threatened the GOP’s chances.

Bresnahan said the Trump administration needs to “figure out a way to securely reopen the strait and bring a resolution, and I'm hoping there is a diplomatic solution quickly.”

He would welcome campaigning with the president, he added, but acknowledged his popularity has taken a hit.

“I think he would be a lot more popular, by a landslide number, once we could bring a resolution to Iran and get fuel prices back to a reasonable area,” the congressman said.

That doesn’t show signs of happening quickly now, with the election just over a month away. So Cognetti is left to press her advantage.

At the brewery, Cognetti went table by table to chat with everyone over beers and pizza. At one point, she talked up her plan to open primary elections to independent voters.

“I promise you that I will fight in Washington, D.C., anyone who is going to put us at risk, anyone who thinks that a rigged system is OK,” she said during her speech. “I’ve taken on our local Democrats up in Scranton. I will take on anyone in D.C.”
entries.author: Alex Roarty

entries.title: White House Officials Told the DOJ to Delay Action on Abortion Ahead of the Midterms
entries.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche has moved slowly in abortion pill litigation and department officials have told advocates to wait until after the election.
entries.content:
The White House has instructed the Justice Department to move slowly on any abortion-related actions ahead of the midterm elections, The Washington Sun has learned.

In a series of discussions, senior White House officials, led by White House chief of staff Susan Wiles, directly delivered the message to Attorney General Todd Blanche, according to a senior administration official not authorized to discuss the matter publicly. Wiles suggested that an aggressive approach on abortion would generate unwanted attention, something the officials worried could alienate voters ahead of the November elections.

“No one wants us taking any real action before the midterms,” the senior administration official said, emphasizing the push came directly from top White House staff.

The White House denied that meetings took place: “This is completely false. These conversations never occurred between White House officials and DOJ officials.”

But administration officials have also informed anti-abortion leaders, who have aggressively pressed the administration to move quickly to restrict abortion access, that any action on abortion would take place after the midterm elections, multiple sources told The Sun.

“Once the midterms are over and it’s truly lame-duck time, we’ve heard the gloves will be off,” one conservative in touch with the administration, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations, said. “We have heard we have friends, and there are definitely people who are staunch pro-lifers.”

The DOJ has consistently asked federal judges to pause ongoing lawsuits that seek to restrict access to the abortion drug mifepristone until the Food and Drug Administration completes a review of the drug’s safety and effectiveness. A departure from that strategy would create unfavorable headlines just before voters head to the polls, the White House officials made clear to Blanche.

The Supreme Court in 2024 dismissed a case that sought to ban the abortion pill mifepristone on procedural grounds. The justices have never taken a position on whether the pills should be available.

Other cases challenging abortion pill access that have emerged since are currently making their way through the federal courts. The Trump administration is defending FDA rules that allow these drugs to be available via mail, but is doing so only on procedural grounds rather than expressly supporting the current regulations. Anti-abortion groups and allies of the movement have urged the DOJ to drop its procedural defense of FDA and, instead, allow courts to rule more quickly on the merits of the cases.

The senior administration official said the White House has made clear to Blanche that it would not support such a strategy.

In response to questions about meetings between Blanche and White House officials, a DOJ spokesperson called President Donald Trump “the most pro-life president in history.” The spokesperson did not answer questions specifically about the meetings or the substance of those meetings.

“The Department of Justice represents [the Food and Drug Administration] in these matters, and FDA is continuing to review the safety data for mifepristone,” the spokesperson said. “We asked the courts to stay these cases while that review is ongoing. Should the Department learn of possible fraud or harm to women involving these drugs, we will investigate those matters.”

Anti-abortion leaders expect post-election action that is not just related to litigation.

A source familiar with the matter said DOJ officials have told some anti-abortion leaders that any action on enforcing the Comstock Act — which would bar the mailing of abortion drugs — would take place after the election.

The DOJ is “actively working on it,” the source said.

Tom McClusky, director of government affairs for CatholicVote, said he has heard “the same thing from every agency I talk to and from members of Congress.” He added, "It’s always that nothing’s going to happen until November."

Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, told The Sun in May that she had “encouraging” meetings with a DOJ official, whom she declined to name, on the Comstock Act. Specifically, she said there are discussions around rescinding a 2022 memo from the Office of Legal Counsel issued during the Biden administration that effectively made the law unenforceable.

But when asked whether the DOJ had given the organization an update as to when action would take place, Kristi Hamrick, vice president of media and policy for Students for Life, told The Sun: “Everything but the election is pushed until after the elections.”

Blanche, in his July confirmation hearings, said he opposed abortion pills being available via mail and committed to enforcing the Comstock Act, a series of 1873 federal laws that prohibit the shipment of “every article or thing designed, adapted or intended for producing abortion.” Politico also reported that during an August call with faith leaders, Blanche said the administration was working to ensure abortion was banned “in every single state.”

As a result, some in the anti-abortion camp are holding out hope that Blanche will be an ally to them.

"Based on Attorney General Blanche's testimony during his confirmation, we have hope and are expecting that swift action will be taken to stop mail-order abortion drugs that are undermining pro-life state laws across the country,” said Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America. “Every day that goes by more women are coerced and harmed and more unborn children die. We are past due for action."

But Blanche has said nothing publicly about abortion since the summer.

A directive from the White House to the DOJ to inject electoral politics into litigation would historically have been seen as highly unusual, at best. In the wake of Watergate, then-Attorney General Benjamin Civiletti issued a memo in 1979 that laid out guidelines to firewall DOJ from White House personnel on certain sensitive matters. That memo, which has become known as the "no contacts" policy, has been updated and strengthened several times in the intervening decades, though Trump loosened it at the start of his current term.

Any action to restrict abortion pills would immediately break Trump’s 2024 campaign pledge that he would “not block” access to the drugs.

The White House first made its intentions for the midterms clear to cabinet members in February, the senior administration official said. Blanche was deputy attorney general at that time but was brought up to speed after he became acting attorney general in April.

The Trump administration’s silence on abortion pills has frustrated even judges overseeing abortion pill cases.

Earlier this month, during oral arguments for Louisiana v. FDA, judges in the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals multiple times pressed DOJ lawyers to state the administration’s perspective on the FDA’s regulations — to no avail.

“The only thing I can say, your honor, is what we’ve said in the briefs, which is that FDA is conducting an ongoing review. It has committed to do this. It’s doing it in an ongoing fashion, so we just haven’t taken a position,” said Daniel Winik, an attorney for the DOJ’s senior counsel.

In response, Judge Stephen Higginson said: “I find that very, very unsatisfactory that the agency won't give an opinion as to its own regulations.”
entries.author: Eric Katz, Oriana González

entries.title: In ‘Swingiest County,’ a Republican Brand Faces Its Toughest Test in 20 Years
entries.summary: The Fitzpatricks haven’t lost a race since 2006. Is this the year Democrats finally break through?
entries.content:
FAIRLESS HILLS, Pa. — Bob Harvie faces an opponent with a who’s who of endorsements from liberal groups that usually back Democrats: the Service Employees International Union, the AFL-CIO, the largest teachers union and two of the most prominent environmental groups.

Harvie isn’t some right-wing conservative. He is a lifelong Democrat squaring off against the most moderate Republican in Congress, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

Harvie’s job is to convince voters, despite their long affinity for the congressman and his late brother who represented this battleground for four terms, that after 10 years on Capitol Hill, Fitzpatrick is different now — and not in a good way.

A new ad this week highlights how Fitzpatrick owns a rental property in California, that he cast a decisive vote on the first version of President Donald Trump’s massive policy bill last summer and voted with Republican leaders on a procedural vote that delayed the release of the Epstein files.

“Congress changed Fitzpatrick. Now, it’s time we change Congress,” Harvie says, concluding the ad.

The incumbent is not taking any of this sitting down. Instead of the more placid campaigns of recent years, which focused mostly on positive image enhancement, Fitzpatrick has unleashed a multimillion-dollar barrage of negative ads that accuse Harvie of voting for a pay hike as county commissioner, along with hints of corruption in a previous local office.

He tells voters that he is every bit the independent-minded Republican they’ve known well, painting Harvie as an overly ambitious politician who “doesn’t relate to the middle-class” voters who dominate this Philadelphia suburb.

“I personally feel very, very close to my district,” Fitzpatrick told The Washington Sun in an hour-long interview this week. “I’m more present than him by a factor of 10.”

Fitzpatrick could be considered the last of a dying breed in Congress, the liberal northeastern Republicans. He descends from a lineage of 25 to 30 years ago when Connie Morella of Maryland, Nancy Johnson and Chris Shays of Connecticut, Charlie Bass of New Hampshire and Sherwood Boehlert of New York had a big presence inside the Republican caucus. They were proud supporters of lower taxes while backing liberal social policies and programs.

One by one they were wiped out politically as their suburban bastions recoiled at the increasingly rightward lean of the national Republican Party.

Recently elected Republicans from that region — Reps. Mike Lawler and Nick LaLota of New York, Jen Kiggans of Virginia and Ryan Mackenzie and Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania — are more conservative and outwardly confrontational than their predecessors.

It’s left Fitzpatrick feeling increasingly isolated, particularly after he worked to round up the 10 key Republican votes in late 2021 to pass then-President Joe Biden’s infrastructure package. He faced so much hostility from fellow Republicans that he has refused ever since to attend the weekly conference meetings Republicans hold for internal deliberations.

He is a self-admitted Republican in name only.

“I’m a registered Republican. There’s a difference,” he told The Sun. If Pennsylvania allowed independents to vote in primaries, Fitzpatrick said he would leave the Republican fold and register as an independent.

“Right now, I’m homeless,” he said.

This homeless politician has always faced headwinds. Trump lost his district in 2016, 2020 and 2024, and in 2018 and 2022, Democrats won the governor’s race by 18 and 20 percentage points, respectively, in Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District.

Yet Fitzpatrick really only had one close election, the 2018 midterms, when he won by just over 2.5 percentage points. Now, however, the state’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, is expected to match or exceed his 2022 margin in this district in what has turned into a cakewalk reelection campaign.

The popular governor has set his sights on flipping at least three state Senate seats and taking full Democratic control of the General Assembly, for his Harrisburg ambitions. And he’s working hard to flip up to four U.S. House seats in Pennsylvania to win a Democratic majority and burnish his national credentials for a possible 2028 presidential campaign.

Three targeted state Senate races are in the 1st Congressional District, and all three Democratic campaign offices in Bucks County are shared with staff for Shapiro, Harvie and the state legislative candidates.

Harvie realizes that, despite losing this district, Trump received close to 50% in each race and that he can’t try to just highlight things Democrats consider scandals.

“It's not just about, ‘Oh, I'm mad about what he said on “Access Hollywood.”’ Whatever that was. I mean, obviously, people clearly don't care about that, and that's something that — we just have to kind of focus on the issues that do matter to them,” he told The Sun during an hour-long interview Saturday at his campaign office here in lower Bucks County.

So instead the Democrat is focusing on the Republican-led Congress letting health-care tax subsidies lapse and how notifications have gone out talking about a more than 15% increase in health costs next year.

Harvie dismisses those endorsements Fitzpatrick can tout as the groups’ efforts to show some tiny measure of bipartisanship, rewarding the incumbent for a few votes while overlooking some key times he gave conservatives a big win.

“That's what Brian gets. He gets a participation trophy,” Harvie said. “He shows up. He's the least bad Republican.”

While Fitzpatrick voted against the final version of what Trump hailed as the One Big Beautiful Bill, Harvie’s campaign points out that he voted for the initial version of the legislation that included those permanent tax cuts for the wealthy and even a provision meant to clamp down on local officials’ ability to regulate data centers.

“He's hiding from his record, and we're not going to let him hide from his record,” Harvie said.

A sign hanging in the campaign office shows two sides of Fitzpatrick, calling him: “Two-faced Fitzpatrick, votes MAGA, not moderate.”
Anti-Fitzpatrick ad (4032x3024, AR: 1.33)In fact, road signs have become a surprisingly dominant theme in the race, a trip back in time where the locals discuss the content of the signs as much as the TV ads.

On one major intersection, Harvie supporters will have each corner covered with a simple white sign and black letters: “Fitzpatrick voted 7 TIMES to RAISE grocery prices.”

Drive a block or two, the next major intersection is blanketed with small white signs from Fitzpatrick backers, with the same black lettering: “Bob Harvie voted HIMSELF a pay raise.”

By June 30, Fitzpatrick had already spent more than $4.8 million on the race, about 60% more than he spent in the entire 2022 midterm campaign. Harvie had spent a quarter of the incumbent’s total at that point, stewarding his resources for the final five-week sprint to Election Day.

Unlike past election years, there’s no Senate race, no presidential campaign and not a competitive governor’s race to dominate TV screens.

Fitzpatrick’s race is getting more attention than ever before in the Philadelphia media market, even if independent political handicappers still rate it a “lean” or “likely” Republican seat.

His brother, Mike Fitzpatrick, first won the district in 2004 but lost in the 2006 midterms when a Middle East war and corruption allegations created a terrible environment for Republicans. He won the seat back in 2010 and coasted to two easy reelections, before deciding to retire after 2016.

That’s when Brian Fitzpatrick quit his FBI job in California and moved home to follow in his brother’s footsteps. The only thing different on the campaign signs was the first name, and his career was launched.

The older brother’s most important piece of advice was to never think about his own ideological position on a vote, nor worry about Trump’s position.

“I take him out of the equation,” Brian Fitzpatrick said.

That’s the ethos that has led him to support same-sex marriage, banning assault weapons, supporting Biden’s infrastructure plan and becoming the first Republican congressional candidate to win the endorsement of the Natural Resources Defense Council.

“They support me because I support their issues,” he told The Sun.

Harvie labeled it a mirage wrapped inside a brand identity that is facing its toughest test with this district’s swing voters.

“They're tired of what has been called Facebook Fitz. You know, he'll show up on Facebook, he'll throw out the first pitch of a Little League game, but when it comes to holding an in-person town hall, he hasn't done one in nine years,” he said.

So far the incumbent has not agreed to a debate, with Democrats saying he is hiding behind the negative commercials as a shield.

To Fitzpatrick, he hasn’t changed at all over the past decade. Instead, he said, “the two parties have become cults.”

Fitzpatrick considers his support for the law to allow independent voters into primaries in all 50 states a defining position for the future.

If he can pull off another victory, he will continue on as a self-proclaimed RINO.

“I am an independent who is registered Republican,” he said.
entries.author: Paul Kane

entries.title: Red States Are Trending Blue. Is Mississippi Really on the Table?
entries.summary: Democrats hope a tanking president, a sour economy and a strong candidate will turn the GOP bastion into the next Georgia.
entries.content:
It’s no secret Republicans are facing a difficult political environment that has boosted Democrats’ hopes of winning the Senate and expanded the battleground map deeper into conservative territory.

But Mississippi?

Even the most optimistic Democrats scoffed at the idea of a competitive race in the ruby-red state going into this campaign cycle. But voters’ anxiety about the economy has deepened, their opinions of President Donald Trump have tanked, and appeals for help from Mississippi Democrats have elevated the idea that Democrat Scott Colom has a chance to oust GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in November.

Now high-profile Democrats are paying visits to the Republican bastion and urging party bosses to send scarce financial resources to Colom’s campaign, hoping to put into play a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in more than four decades.

“I think he's got a real shot,” said Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock, an early supporter who flipped a red seat in Georgia in 2020. “We should spend more money there.”

Although Mississippi remains a heavily Republican state, Colom has run a surprisingly competitive campaign. The local district attorney has gotten endorsements from other prominent Democrats such as former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, who’s scheduled to campaign with Colom on Friday in Mississippi.

Hyde-Smith this week began airing ads attacking Colom, generally seen as a sign she’s taking the race seriously.

Democrats believe the senator has reason to worry. Some see Mississippi as the next Georgia, a sleeper purple state with a large African American population that — if engaged and motivated — can help make Democratic candidates competitive there.

Democrats also believe Hyde-Smith to be particularly vulnerable due to her support for Trump policies that have squeezed Americans, including cuts to Medicaid and SNAP food assistance, tariffs and the Iran war, which has spiked fuel and fertilizer costs for farmers in Mississippi and elsewhere around the country.

There are certainly obstacles. One is the question of turning out Black voters in Mississippi, who have faced historic discrimination and barriers to the ballot box. Republicans this year sought to redraw the state’s 2nd Congressional District to eliminate the state's only majority-Black district and unseat longtime Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. The Supreme Court foiled that effort this month, and Democrats believe it will backfire to the benefit of Colom’s campaign.

“If that increases Mississippi's Black voter turnout significantly, and if he's only just a few points back, boom — you've now closed the gap, and you're in the game,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) said.

Colom’s campaign has also put a spotlight on Hyde-Smith’s decision in 2023 to block Colom from receiving a lifetime appointment to a federal judgeship in Mississippi. Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to the post, but Hyde-Smith refused to approve the pick, which effectively killed his nomination.

Republicans think Democrats are dreaming. For now, the incumbent senator is overwhelmingly favored in the race. Trump won the state by 23 percentage points in 2024, and registered Republicans vastly outnumber Democrats there. Mississippi Republicans are also confident they’ll retain the seat even as the party plays defense in other red states, including Texas, Iowa, Ohio, Alaska and Kansas.

“They always have a chance, but we’re going to win,” Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) said of the Democratic odds on Wednesday.

While Democratic campaigns held a financial advantage over the summer, Republicans and their affiliated super PACs are now outspending Democratic Senate candidates all over the country. Democrats’ cash crunch is compounded by pressure to invest everywhere, including most recently in the battleground Texas Senate race.

In Mississippi, national Democrats and their affiliated super PACs haven’t yet committed resources, but they are signaling to donors to open their wallets. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York), who chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, headlined an event for Colom in New York City earlier this month, a source familiar with the event told The Sun. The source also said that Gillibrand has maxed out her contributions to Colom’s campaign.

Colom argues Democrats are making a mistake by not investing in Mississippi since doing so now could also bolster their chances of flipping the seat in the future.

“We've not won in Mississippi because we're not trying,” he told The Washington Sun in an interview. “You got 38% of the population African American voters, 90% who are Democrat. Got 15% at minimum, on average, white voters who are gonna vote Democrat. You only need to get 10[%] more of the white voters.”

“If you can't compete in a state like that, you need to ask yourself, what's wrong with you? Right? Like, what is wrong with your message? What is wrong with your strategy?’ he said.

“Look at the math,” he said. “The math is why it's possible, and it's just shameful that we haven't been trying.”
entries.author: Igor Bobic

entries.title: Maryland High Schools Are Navigating a ‘Bell to Bell’ Cellphone Ban
entries.summary: Montgomery County students and parents have flagged “inconsistencies” in the rollout of the strict new rules.
entries.content:
Montgomery County high schools are navigating “inconsistencies” in the rollout of a new policy banning students’ cellphone use not only in class, but in the hallways and during lunch.

Five weeks into the academic year, some students are complaining that the restrictions go too far, while school officials seek a uniform answer to a basic question: Where do you store all the phones?

The “bell to bell” ban in high schools is different from last year, when students could pull out their phones in the corridors or during lunch period to check in with parents or friends, or engage on social media.

The issue for the county school system isn’t so much the policy itself, but what “phone-free” actually looks like — and the uneven, sometimes awkward process of enforcing it.

Adam Van Grack, a Rockville Council member whose son attends Wootton High School, said he understands that teachers should not have to compete with phones for attention. But he is ambivalent about an absolute ban, at least until the details are finalized.

Van Grack said he views the issue “through a slightly different lens” after a nonfatal shooting at Wootton last year, when the school was placed on lockdown. Van Grack’s son was in a barricaded classroom, and “I cannot overstate how important it was to me, as his father, to be able to text with him, to hear directly from him that he was OK, and to stay connected with him.”

Apprised of the council member’s comments, the school district sent The Washington Sun a fact sheet emphasizing that the county permits student cellphone use during emergencies. It is up to the school principal to temporarily lift the ban.

Among Van Grack’s concerns is making sure students’ phones can be accessed if urgently needed.

During nonemergencies, MCPS schools use a variety of systems to help keep the devices out of students' hands, including storing them in lockers, classroom caddies with slots for individual phones, or pouches that typically remain locked during school hours.

The fact sheet, which was sent by the school district to families, said the ban applies to “class time, lunch, recess, and passing periods like walking in the hallway or using the restroom.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The memo didn’t specify where the phones would be kept, and some students say it’s easiest to carry the devices with them unless a teacher objects. Some teachers require students to place phones in a “caddy” with slots to accommodate as many as 30 devices.

“I normally keep it in my backpack,” said Audrey Elsasser, an Einstein High School sophomore. “Technically, it can be in your pocket but if they see it in your hand, that’s a problem. If you want to go to the bathroom, then you have to give them your phone.”

Ryan Aleman Reyes, a Walter Johnson High School senior, said: “We’re almost not even restrained on what we can do.”

Unless he is taking a test, Reyes said he has never been told to store his phone in a classroom caddy or locker. “Perhaps in some other classes, they have to do that, but I haven’t had to,” he said.

Jonah Mishalove, a senior and president of the Student Government Association at Bethesda-Chevy Chase High School, has had a different experience.

“There are phone pouches on the wall of each class, you are assigned a number on the first day, and you keep your phone in that number,” Mishalove said. “I'd say every teacher implements it. Some are a bit more lax about it.”

For example, he said, a teacher might permit a student to walk up to the pouch and “text your parents about a doctor’s appointment or something. But for the most part, you walk in, put your phone up. And then at the end, you take your phone and go to your next class.”

Under a Maryland state law passed in the last legislative session, each county Board of Education in the state is required to implement by the 2027-28 school year a policy prohibiting the use of smartphones and similar devices during the school day. Exceptions were made for students needing their phone because of a disability, health issue or to access language translation platforms or meet caregiving responsibilities.

Montgomery, the state’s largest county, opted to proceed a year early “in the interest of reducing distractions to teaching and learning,” said MCPS spokeswoman Liliana Lopez.

Asked about the variety of phone storage options, she said: “We expect to have worked through implementation inconsistencies before the state requirement takes effect next school year.”

Students violating the policy can have their phones confiscated for the day, with repeated violations subject to escalating disciplinary measures. Lopez said she didn’t have data on how many students’ phones had been taken away.

The ban includes tablets, smartwatches, AirPods, and other devices that connect to the internet.

The Sun requested interviews with five high school principals around the county to assess the transition to the new policy, but Lopez said the district wanted to complete the “implementation phase” before granting interviews.

Montgomery County’s middle and elementary schools already prohibited students from using the devices during the school day, so their policies did not need to be adjusted this year.

Across the country, schools are taking a harder line on student cellphones.

While most states have laws restricting cellphone use in schools, “probably a third or so of schools” nationwide have gone as far as Maryland in prohibiting the devices for the entire day, said Brian Jacob, a University of Michigan education policy and economics professor.

In many states, the rules are as simple as telling students their phones must not be visible. “I think the challenge with most of these no-show policies is that they’re hard to enforce, and the onus of enforcement really rests on individual teachers,” Jacob said.

Elsasser, the Einstein student, said she understands the need for cellphone restrictions in class, but considers it “unreasonable” to have extended the ban into lunch.

“It’s very unpopular,” Elsasser said. “It has nothing to do with focusing on school because you’re not doing schoolwork.”

Mishalove, the B-CC student, said the cellphone policy as a whole “is helpful for creating a good learning environment.”

But he agreed that the lunch period ban “is definitely something that should be looked at. I’ve been kind of communicating a little bit with our administration about that. I personally don’t see how that [restriction] is super helpful.”
entries.author: Jeff Barker
